ingredients.intro: The listing names the species and, unusually for this shelf, the part of the tree as well. Here is the tree, the bark, and the figures the label still leaves out.

cards.alt: A pau d'arco tree in full pink flower on open dry ground
cards.p: A forest tree of Brazil, Paraguay and northern Argentina that flowers pink on bare branches before it comes into leaf, which is what the photograph shows. The bark is what the trade takes, under the names pau d'arco, ipe roxo and lapacho. It is the same tree that opens the ingredient list of Decolonise.

cards.alt: Dried strips of pau d'arco inner bark
cards.p: The inner bark is the living layer just under the surface, and it is the part the trade asks for by name. Our listing prints it, which puts this jar ahead of several others on the same shelf where the part of the plant is simply a blank. The photograph is of dried bark of the species rather than of anything in our sacks.

cards.alt: Clove buds, black peppercorns and a pale flecked powder in three small bowls on a wooden sill, a generated scene
cards.p: Bark, dried and milled. The listing prints no milligrams a capsule and no capsule count, so there is no serving weight and no cost a day on the sheet below. The bowls in the picture are a generated scene and none of the powder in them is ours.

cards.alt: Two plain capsules on a saucer beside a glass of water, a generated scene
cards.p: The listing prints 100 per cent vegan, wildcrafted, non GMO and additive free. It does not name the shell material, so the sheet does not name one. The capsules in the picture are a generated scene rather than a photograph of ours.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named, the part of the tree is named, and the accepted binomial sits next to the one on the jar so that you can look it up under either. The two figures we do not have, the count and the milligrams, are named as missing rather than estimated. What pau d'arco does in a person is not something we are permitted to say, so it is not on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: The bark, and the name it lost
paras: This jar says Tabebuia impetiginosa and the botanists say Handroanthus impetiginosus. The genus was split in 2007 and a large part of Tabebuia moved across, but the trade never followed, so the old name is still what you will find on nearly every sack of this bark in the world. Both names are the same tree. I print both, because you should be able to look it up under either one and land in the same place.

What I like about this label is that it says inner bark. That sounds like nothing. It is the one thing most bark labels leave out, and it is the difference between the living layer just under the surface, which is what the trade actually asks for, and whatever came off the outside of the log. Several other jars on this shelf will not tell you which part of the plant is in them. This one does, and I would rather praise a label for that than pretend it is normal.

What it does not tell you is how many capsules are in the jar, how many milligrams are in each of them, or how long a course is meant to run. So there is no cost a day here, and if you are thinking about taking it for months rather than weeks, ring the counter and ask, because the label will not answer you and neither will this page.
reiss.pull: Inner bark. It sounds like nothing, and it is the one thing most bark labels leave out.
